title: ASP.NET Core API latency increased 40x after a deployment
description: Diagnose a 40x latency regression in an ASP.NET Core API after deployment by investigating middleware, DI container behavior, compilation settings, and database access patterns.

data.text: After deploying a minor update to an ASP.NET Core API, p95 latency jumps from 120ms to 5 seconds. CPU usage is normal, memory is stable, and the health check endpoint responds quickly. The regression affects only authenticated endpoints. You need to find the bottleneck using ASP.NET Core diagnostics and fix it without reverting the deployment.

items: Synchronous I/O introduced in a new middleware or controller action blocks the thread pool
A new scoped service was registered as singleton, causing memory leaks and GC pressure
Database queries without indexes or with N+1 fetching patterns after an ORM model change
JSON serialization options changed to include reference loops, causing massive payload sizes
Response caching was disabled accidentally during the deployment
A new authentication handler makes remote calls on every request without caching

terms.definition: Software that sits between the server and application logic, processing requests and responses in a pipeline.
The scope of a registered service: transient, scoped, or singleton. Misconfigured lifetimes cause memory leaks and thread safety bugs.
The cross-platform web server for ASP.NET Core, responsible for accepting connections and passing requests to the middleware pipeline.
Blocking operations that hold a thread while waiting for I/O to complete, exhausting the thread pool under load.
Compile-time code generation in .NET that can improve startup performance by pre-generating serialization and routing code.

items: Enable ASP.NET Core diagnostics and collect metrics from DiagnosticListener
Use dotnet-trace or Visual Studio Profiler to capture a 30-second trace during the latency spike
Inspect the trace for synchronous I/O calls: .Result, .Wait(), or .GetAwaiter().GetHandle()
Check dependency injection registrations in Program.cs for lifetime mismatches
Review database query plans for new queries introduced in the deployment
Compare middleware pipeline order between the previous and current release

data.title: Sync-over-async is a silent killer
data.text: Calling .Result or .Wait() on an async method in ASP.NET Core blocks a thread pool thread. Under load, this exhausts the thread pool and causes request queuing. Always use async/await all the way down.

data.title: Profile an ASP.NET Core API for latency
data.description: Take a sample ASP.NET Core API and introduce a latency regression by adding synchronous I/O. Then use dotnet-trace to find it.
steps: Create or clone a small ASP.NET Core Web API project
Add a controller action that calls an async method with .Result
Run the API and generate load with a tool like k6 or Apache Bench
Capture a trace with dotnet-trace collect --providers Microsoft-AspNetCore-Server-Kestrel
Identify the blocking call in the trace and fix it to async/await
data.expectedOutcome: You should see thread pool starvation in the trace and a measurable latency drop after fixing the sync-over-async call.

data.title: Summary
points: Compare middleware and DI registration changes between releases first
Use async/await all the way down to avoid thread pool starvation
Profile with dotnet-trace rather than guessing from metrics alone
Verify the fix in a canary deployment before rolling out to all instances
data.takeaway: In ASP.NET Core, the most common cause of post-deployment latency is not the database; it is blocking asynchronous code in the request pipeline.
